catalog_locator: Sec. 2.1 'Phonemic inventory and chart', p. 6 (PDF p. 6; page render); sec. 2.2 'The vowel e', p. 7 (PDF p. 7); p. 8 top
catalog_quote: [p.6] While work remains to be done on a final phonemic statement for Inati, a preliminary assessment by Tezuka (1983) lists 19 consonant phonemes (p, t, k, ʔ, b, d, g, s, ts, š, h, ž, m, n, ng, l, r, y, and w) and 5 vowel phones (i, ü, o, a, and ä). Data on stress and vowel length were presented with no conclusions, e.g. bohiʔ 'alive' and bo:hiʔ 'to release', ˈanay, 'termite' and anáy 'to wait'. Minimal pairs contrasting these consonants and vowels are given except for ts, š, and ž. [...] [p.7] There are exceptions: karaye 'their' and wayte 'that, you'. But a rule involving stress and glides is a factor. Tezuka (1983:8) mentions that there are "cases when w and y occur syllable finally in CVC and receive a stress." He limits this to four words: kay.ti 'this' kay.ni 'that' kay.nad 'that' kaw.ni 'a while ago'. But way.te and karay.e might also be included. Therefore, stress on the glides…

Sec. 2 'Phonology', 2.1 'Phonemic inventory and chart', p.6 reads exactly as quoted: 'While work remains to be done on a final phonemic statement for Inati, a preliminary assessment by Tezuka (1983) lists 19 consonant phonemes (p, t, k, ʔ, b, d, g, s, ts, š, h, ž, m, n, ng, l, r, y, and w) and 5 vowel phones (i, ü, o, a, and ä). Data on stress and vowel length were presented with no conclusions, e.g. bohiʔ 'alive' and bo:hiʔ 'to release', ˈanay 'termite' and anáy 'to wait'.' (the printed page has a raised stress tick before the first anay and an acute on the s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand published statement says stress and vowel length were recorded but not analysed; the illustrative pairs (ˈanay 'termite' vs anáy 'to wait'; bohiʔ vs bo:hiʔ) imply that stress/length position is contrastive (initial~penult vs final on disyllables), i.e. lexically specified as in neighbouring Bisayan languages, but the author explicitly draws no conclusion. Later transcriptions (Lobel 2013 accent marks; Manzano 2021 IPA) likewise show both penultimate and final stress without comment.
new_statements.exceptions: Tezuka (via Pennoyer p.7): CVC syllables closed by a glide (kay-, kaw-) attract stress in four deictic/temporal words; Pennoyer adds wayte, karaye and suggests 'stress on the glides may overrule vowel harmony'.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms (word level); data from the Inete dialect of Nagpana, Barotac Viejo, Iloilo. Vowel length and stress are not disentangled (bo:hiʔ written with length, anáy with stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Pennoyer's phonology section describes Inete, the Iloilo dialect (Nagpana, Barotac Viejo), which he labels 'Inati'; Sogodnin is the moribund northern (Aklan/Boracay/Carabao) dialect. Manzano 2021 describes the Numancia (Aklan) variety. All fall under atii1237 (no separate Glottolog dialect codes). Tezuka's ms title says 'Inata' but concerns the Nagpana Ati of Panay, not the Ata of Negros (ataa1240).

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 p.6: Tezuka's (1983) preliminary phonemic statement presented 'data on stress and vowel length.. with no conclusions', citing pairs bohiʔ 'alive' vs bo:hiʔ 'to release', ˈanay 'termite' vs anáy 'to wait'; p.7 quotes Tezuka (1983:8) that glides w/y 'occur syllable finally in CVC and receive a stress' (kay.ti, kay.ni, kay.nad, kaw.ni) and suggests 'stress on the glides may overrule vowel harmony'; p.8 a passing remark on final stress of inom. No rule for stress placement; Appendix wordlists carry no stress marks.

sources.note: No statement on Inati accent. Inati forms are written with Tagalog-style accent diacritics (fn. 2 p.196: acute = stressed vowel), and the data show both penultimate (káən 'eat', pálad 'hand', lákaw 'walk', dúru 'many', mánok 'chicken', áko 1SG) and final (maisút 'few', bedò.. kaytô, kitô) accent, i.e. lexically varying position, but Lobel does not comment on it for Inati (his contrastive-accent statement in 8.2.9 concerns Manide/Inagta Alabat).
